walkthroughs.body_html:
Trade in the Contemporary World / Global Migration / Human Rights / Power & Borders — a core area of A-Level Geography.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Trade in the Contemporary World / Global Migration / Human Rights / Power & Borders brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Trade in the Contemporary World / Global Migration / Human Rights / Power & Borders.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Is trade between countries a zero-sum game?
options: No — comparative advantage means both partners can gain from specialisation and exchange, though the gains are often shared unevenly between and within countries.
If one country gains from trade, its partner must lose.
Borders are repainted every decade by the UN.
Countries take turns winning at trade each year.

mcqs.q: Do most migrants move from the world's poorest countries to the richest?
options: Countries take turns winning at trade each year.
Migration flows simply run from the poorest nations to the richest.
No — much migration is regional or between developing countries, and the very poorest often cannot afford to move far; emigration commonly rises as incomes initially grow.
Migrants are assigned destinations alphabetically.

mcqs.q: Does state sovereignty mean borders are fixed forever?
options: Countries take turns winning at trade each year.
National borders are permanent natural features.
Borders are repainted every decade by the UN.
No — borders change through treaties, conflict and independence movements, and sovereignty is increasingly contested by supranational bodies, TNCs and global flows.
